newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court rejects Jewish land claim.
newsitem.headline: German court rejects Jewish land claim.

text.p: A German court on Thursday rejected a property claim by a Jewish family which said it had been forced to sell off an area of land below the market rate by the Nazis in the 1930s.

The Potsdam court gave no immediate reason for its decision in the case, which involved 11 properties in the town of Tetlow-Seehof, south of Berlin. The heirs also lay claim to 800 other properties in the area.
Lawyers for the heirs, who now live in the United States, said they would consider an appeal to the Federal Administrative Court after reading the court's opinion.
Jewish families whose property was confiscated or unfairly sold by the Nazis can claim restitution under German law.
Most cases in western Germany were settled long ago but German unification in 1990 has thrown up a series of new claims in the former communist east, where the law did not apply.
The Tetlow-Seehof case, being pursued by the heirs of businessmen Max and Albert Sabersky, was one of the biggest such claims and was expected to set the tone for similar cases in the east.
Lawyers for the heirs and the local property-owners have been trying to resolve the claims for around six years.
The local government agency responsible for resolving property issues had rejected the Sabersky claims, saying it believed the businessmen received a fair price for their land.
"I'm thrilled about the decision. After six years, the court has finally decided to let these people live in peace and quiet," said Josephine Ewers, an official with the agency.
"I hope this sends a signal to the Federal Administrative Court," she added. "We never accepted that this was a case of Nazi persecution".
